items.passage:
Nargis would not look at me across the yard,
where bamboo ribs lay drying in the sun
and paper skins hung waiting to be glued.
I had told the neighbors that the string
had simply snapped, that no one was to blame.
She knew I let it go. She saw my hand.
All week she worked in silence by the wall,
her needle plain and steady, never quick,
and every kite she finished bore one seam
left bare, unpainted, where the tear had been.
She would not argue; she would not forgive
the tidy story I had made of it.
Her craft, I learned, was patient and ______:
it hid no flaw, and so it showed me mine.
Ruwan, she wrote at last beneath one frame,
and left the empty space for me to fill.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: ornamental
hesitant
candid
forgiving
items.explanation: 화자 Ruwan은 사고를 '줄이 그냥 끊어졌다'고 꾸며 말했고, Nargis는 찢어진 자리를 칠하지 않은 솔기로 그대로 드러낸다. 빈칸 뒤 '어떤 결함도 숨기지 않았다'는 설명과 앞의 '맨 솔기' 묘사를 연결하면 '솔직한'을 뜻하는 C가 가장 정확하다. A는 장식적이라는 뜻으로 꾸밈없는 솔기와 반대되고, B는 '바늘이 꾸준했다'는 묘사와 맞지 않는다. D는 Nargis가 '용서하지 않았다'는 문장과 충돌한다.

items.passage: Three rules governed the old harbor-light station my family rented on the Danube bank outside Vienna: no boots upstairs, no lamps lit before dusk, and no questions about the photograph in the stairwell. Felix, the landlord's son, enforced the third rule most strictly. Whenever I paused before the faded print of two boys standing beside the lens, he would hurry me along. One evening, though, I found Anselm, my father's elderly friend, studying it with me. He tapped the smaller boy and said nothing. Later Felix admitted that the boy was his uncle, who had drowned the winter the photograph was taken, and that his family had never once spoken his name aloud. I understood then that the rule was not about privacy at all. Felix's silence was not indifference but a kind of ______, a way of guarding something too fragile to be handled by strangers.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: distrustfulness
carelessness
resentment
protectiveness
items.explanation: Felix는 사진에 대한 질문을 금하는 규칙을 가장 엄격히 지키고, 나중에 사진 속 소년이 물에 빠져 죽은 삼촌임을 털어놓는다. 빈칸 뒤 '낯선 사람이 다루기에 너무 연약한 것을 지키는 방식'이라는 설명과 연결하면 '보호하려는 마음'인 D가 가장 정확하다. A는 그가 화자를 의심했다는 근거가 없고, B는 규칙을 엄격히 지킨 태도와 반대다. C는 그럴듯하지만 분노나 원망을 보여 주는 단서는 지문에 없다.

items.passage: Paper envelopes of teff and sorghum lined the cooperative's shelves in Addis Ababa, each labeled in my mother's slanted hand. I was sorting them when Kagiso, my brother's tutor, came in with the news that our friend Meseret had only weeks left. I wanted to tell her the truth: that the drought had ruined the seed plot she had spent her last strong summer planting. Kagiso shook his head. He did not lie to students, he said, but he believed some truths could wait for a gentler season. I argued with him all afternoon. Yet when I visited Meseret, I found myself describing only the envelopes we had saved, the varieties that would outlast us both. I did not invent a harvest, but I chose which facts to carry into her room. My honesty that day was not abandoned; it was ______, trimmed to what she could hold.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: selective
deceptive
reluctant
exhaustive
items.explanation: 화자 Aster는 처음에는 진실을 모두 말하려 했지만, 친구에게 거짓 수확을 지어내지 않으면서도 '어떤 사실을 가져갈지 골랐다'고 말한다. 빈칸 뒤 '그녀가 감당할 수 있는 만큼 다듬어졌다'는 설명까지 연결하면 '선별적인'인 A가 정확하다. B는 '수확을 지어내지 않았다'는 문장과 충돌하고, D는 일부 사실만 전했다는 내용과 반대다. C는 그럴듯하지만 망설임보다 의도적인 선택이 강조된다.

items.passage: Beulah never lost a contest she meant to win. So when the whole South Side heard that Odessa had beaten her at the church sewing fair, people came to the tailor's back room just to see her face. They found Beulah calmly pressing a hem, humming. Odessa came too, every day for a week, asking the same question: why had Beulah left a crooked seam on the sleeve the judges examined? Beulah only smiled and threaded another needle. At last, on the seventh day, she unfolded Odessa's prize ribbon from the drawer where Odessa had tossed it in shame. "You needed that blue more than I did," Beulah said. "Your shop was closing. Mine was not." Odessa held the ribbon a long time. Like the fox in the old stories who loses a race to feed a hungry neighbor, Beulah had been ______ in defeat, giving away a victory she could easily have kept.
items.question: Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
options: heedless
generous
resentful
boastful
items.explanation: Beulah는 원하면 언제나 이기는 사람인데 일부러 비뚤어진 솔기를 남겨 Odessa에게 승리를 넘겼고, 그 이유는 Odessa의 가게가 문을 닫을 처지였기 때문이다. 빈칸 뒤 '쉽게 지킬 수 있었던 승리를 내주었다'는 설명과 연결하면 '너그러운'인 B가 정확하다. A는 일부러 진 것이라 부주의와 다르고, C는 그녀가 차분히 콧노래를 불렀다는 묘사와 맞지 않는다. D는 그녀가 일주일 동안 미소만 짓고 말하지 않은 태도와 충돌한다.

items.passage: Seville's heat had already settled over the terrace when Joaquin carried out the last box. Lucius, his mother's name for the half-built birdhouse they had started when he was nine, still sat on the ledge, its roof missing. She teased him about it while he loaded the car: a future engineer who could not finish four walls and a perch. He laughed, and she laughed louder, listing every project he had abandoned, the kite, the radio, the tiled step. Then she picked up the birdhouse and turned it over in her hands. Underneath, in pencil, were the measurements for the roof, written in his childish script and never used. She stopped talking. She set the birdhouse back on the ledge very carefully, as if it might break, and told him she would leave it exactly as it was until he came home to finish it.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From anxious worry about the son's departure to calm acceptance of his choices
From playful teasing about unfinished work to quiet tenderness toward the son
From cheerful pride in the son's skill to open regret over a lost childhood
From mild impatience with the packing to sincere gratitude for the son's help
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 어머니는 아들이 끝내지 못한 새집과 여러 프로젝트를 나열하며 웃으며 놀린다. 새집 밑에서 아들이 어릴 때 적어 둔 지붕 치수를 발견한 뒤 그녀는 말을 멈추고 새집을 조심스럽게 내려놓는다. 따라서 장난스러운 놀림에서 조용한 애정으로 바뀐다는 B가 정답이다. A는 초반의 웃음과 맞지 않고, C는 그녀가 아들의 기술을 자랑하지 않고 오히려 놀렸다는 점에서 틀리며, D는 짐 싸기에 대한 짜증이 나타나지 않는다.

items.passage: By the third evening of the festival, the weaving cooperative in Lisbon had run out of chairs. Larissa, who had not set foot in a church in ten years, watched Father Bruno try to arrange one long table for two groups that had never eaten together: the women who kept the old saint's-day customs and the newer members who kept none. He fussed over place cards, shifting names, and Larissa found it absurd, almost comic, that a priest should worry so much about seating. She whispered as much to the woman beside her. Then she noticed what he was doing. He had placed each older weaver beside a newer one whose pattern she had once criticized, and on every plate he had folded a scrap of the other's cloth. Larissa stopped smiling. She saw that the table had been woven as carefully as any shawl on the loom.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From quiet reverence for the priest to growing doubt about his methods
From open hostility toward the festival to reluctant pleasure in its food
From amused skepticism about the priest's fussing to sober admiration
From weary boredom with the weavers to sudden alarm at their conflict
items.explanation: 처음에 Larissa는 신부가 좌석 배치에 신경 쓰는 모습을 우스꽝스럽다고 여기며 옆 사람에게 속삭인다. 그러나 신부가 서로 비판했던 직조공들을 짝지어 앉히고 상대의 천 조각을 접어 둔 것을 알아챈 뒤 그녀는 웃음을 멈춘다. 따라서 재미 섞인 회의에서 진지한 감탄으로 바뀐다는 C가 정답이다. A는 방향이 반대이고, B는 축제에 대한 적대감이나 음식에 대한 언급이 없으며, D는 그녀가 놀라거나 갈등을 걱정하는 장면이 없다.

items.passage:
I pinned the sheets on Silas's line that spring,
the Cornish wind half wrestling them from me,
and laughed to think how many years we'd spent
at chess-club boards, two old men keeping score
of every bishop lost, each petty win.
He'd beaten me at last the week before.
I meant to tease him over it today.
But in his drawer, beneath the clothespin tin,
I found a notebook of my games, not his,
each losing move of mine marked out in ink
and next to it, in his small careful hand,
the better move, and then: "Show Mabel this."
He never had. The wind went still. I stood
with one white sheet held open in my arms
and folded it as if it were a flag.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From bitter rivalry with Silas to grudging respect for his skill at chess
From solemn grief over Silas to cheerful memories of their old matches
From restless frustration with the wind to calm satisfaction in the chore
From lighthearted rivalry over chess to hushed, reverent recognition
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 바람과 씨름하며 웃고, 체스 경쟁을 '사소한 승리'라 부르며 Silas를 놀릴 생각을 한다. 서랍에서 자신의 패배 수마다 더 나은 수를 적어 둔 공책을 발견한 뒤 바람이 멎고, 화자는 시트를 깃발처럼 접는다. 따라서 가벼운 경쟁심에서 조용하고 경건한 깨달음으로 바뀐다는 D가 정답이다. A는 초반 어조가 쓰라린 적대가 아니라 장난스럽고, B는 방향이 반대이며, C는 체스와 공책이라는 핵심 전환을 놓친다.

items.passage:
ZEYNEP: (holding up a pocket watch) Your grandfather wound this every morning for forty years. And now you want to say goodbye to him with a speech?
APONI: A short one. Something proper. People expect it.
ZEYNEP: People expect sandwiches, too. (She snaps the watch open, grinning.) He'd have fallen asleep by your second sentence.
APONI: (laughing despite himself) He fell asleep at my graduation.
ZEYNEP: Twice. (Her grin fades. She listens to the watch, which has stopped.) He brought it here the week before he died. Asked me to fix it. I told him there was no hurry.
APONI: There wasn't.
ZEYNEP: (quietly, setting the watch on the counter between them) There was. I just didn't hear it. Wind it, child. Not for the speech. Let it run on the plateau a little longer than he did.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From teasing banter about the speech to subdued, remorseful sincerity
From formal politeness between strangers to relaxed, joking familiarity
From sharp anger at the grandson to calm forgiveness of his mistakes
From grieving silence over the death to lively plans for the funeral
items.explanation: 처음에 Zeynep은 연설이 지루할 것이라며 웃으며 농담하고, Aponi도 졸업식 이야기로 함께 웃는다. 그러나 멈춘 시계를 듣는 순간 미소가 사라지고, 수리를 미룬 일을 '나는 듣지 못했다'며 조용히 후회한다. 따라서 장난스러운 대화에서 가라앉은 진지한 후회로 바뀐다는 A가 정답이다. B는 두 사람이 처음부터 친밀하므로 틀리고, C는 Zeynep이 화를 내지 않으며, D는 방향이 반대다.

items.passage: Some alliances arrive disguised. I had spent a month dreading the afternoon Dwayne's aunt Kemoy would join our wedding planning at the salt-water pool in Port of Spain, where my mother and I did our best thinking with our feet in the water. Kemoy had opinions, everyone warned me, and she had opposed the engagement. I rehearsed polite refusals. When she arrived, she criticized the guest list, the menu, the color of the tablecloths, and I felt my mother stiffen beside me. Then Kemoy pulled a folded paper from her bag: the name of a caterer who owed her a favor, a cousin with a free hall, a band that played for half price. She had not come to oppose us. She had come prepared, as she said, to keep two families from going broke on one day. My mother laughed until she nearly slipped into the pool.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From relaxed contentment at the pool to sudden fear of a family quarrel
From tense apprehension about Kemoy to relieved and amused gratitude
From open hostility toward the wedding to quiet acceptance of its costs
From cheerful planning with the mother to weary resignation about money
items.explanation: 화자는 한 달 동안 Kemoy와의 만남을 두려워하며 정중한 거절을 연습했고, 그녀가 하객 명단과 메뉴를 비판하자 어머니까지 긴장한다. 그런데 Kemoy가 출장 요리사, 무료 홀, 반값 밴드 목록을 꺼내자 화자는 그녀가 반대하러 온 것이 아님을 깨닫고, 어머니는 크게 웃는다. 따라서 긴장된 염려에서 안도와 즐거운 감사로 바뀐다는 B가 정답이다. A는 방향이 반대이고, C는 화자가 결혼을 적대한 적이 없으며, D는 결말의 웃음과 맞지 않는다.

items.passage: Years later, I still think of the noodle stall by the harbor in Tromso where my mother, Mattie, and I ate on the night before I left for college. I was sulking. The broth was too salty, the wind too cold, and Soren, the old cook, kept humming the same tuneless song. I complained about all of it, loudly, as if the whole town had arranged itself to annoy me. When we went to pay, Soren waved my mother's money away. He pointed at my suitcase and said his own son had left on a night like this and never once written home. He had made us the soup his son liked best. My mother thanked him, and I said nothing, because I could not. I carried the taste of that salty broth all the way across the ocean, and I wrote home every Sunday.
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the text?
options: From nostalgic warmth about the harbor to bitter regret over leaving home
From cheerful excitement about college to anxious fear of the long trip
From petulant complaint about the meal to humbled, grateful silence
From polite interest in the cook to open suspicion of his kind motives
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 화자는 국물이 짜고 바람이 차며 요리사의 노래가 거슬린다며 큰 소리로 불평한다. Soren이 돈을 받지 않고 떠난 아들 이야기를 하며 아들이 좋아하던 국을 만들었다고 밝히자, 화자는 아무 말도 할 수 없게 된다. 따라서 투정 섞인 불평에서 겸허하고 감사한 침묵으로 바뀐다는 C가 정답이다. A는 쓰라린 후회가 나타나지 않고, B는 화자가 처음부터 들떠 있지 않았으며, D는 요리사를 의심하는 장면이 없다.

items.passage:
"Wrong door again," I muttered, finding your envelope in my dryer at the laundromat this morning.
Dear Talon,
I am writing because this is the third letter of yours that has landed in my machine, my mailbox, or my coat pocket, and I am beginning to suspect the wall between our apartments is thinner than either of us thought. I was ready to slide it under your door with a stern note. I even drafted the note. But the envelope had come open in the wash, and I read the first line before I could stop myself. It was from the hospital, about your sister. I am sorry I read it. I am more sorry that you have been carrying this alone on the other side of a wall I complain about every night. My door is open after six. I will bring the coffee, and I will not mention the mail.
Tallulah
items.question: Which choice best describes the shift in tone that occurs in the letter?
options: From warm friendliness toward Talon to cold formality about the mail
From cheerful amusement at the mix-up to anxious worry about the hospital
From formal apology for reading the letter to playful teasing of Talon
From irritated exasperation over misdelivered mail to gentle compassion
items.explanation: 편지 앞부분에서 Tallulah는 세 번째로 잘못 온 편지에 투덜대며 엄한 쪽지까지 써 두었다고 말한다. 그러나 병원에서 온 Talon의 누나 소식을 읽은 뒤 사과하고, 혼자 짐을 지고 있던 그를 위해 문을 열어 두겠다고 말한다. 따라서 짜증 섞인 불만에서 부드러운 연민으로 바뀐다는 D가 정답이다. A는 방향이 반대이고, B는 초반이 즐거움이 아니라 짜증이며, C는 편지가 장난스러운 놀림으로 끝나지 않는다.

items.passage: We had not spoken in two years when Wenhua appeared at the boarding-house kitchen in Taipei, carrying a sack of shriveled oranges from the orchard our father had left us. The harvest had failed; she had stayed to work it, and I had gone to the city. For a long time neither of us mentioned this. She peeled an orange and complained that the boarders' stove was too small. I complained that the fruit was too sour. Then, almost without meaning to, Mingyu, she said, using the name only our father had used for me, do you remember the year the frost took everything and he made marmalade from the bitter ones anyway? I did remember. We found a pot, a bag of sugar, and the boarders' cracked jars. By midnight the kitchen smelled of burnt peel, and we were arguing again, but about how much sugar to add.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It presents a tense reunion, introduces a shared memory, and then shows the sisters cooperating on a task.
It recounts a failed harvest, explains its causes in some detail, and then describes how the orchard was sold.
It describes a quarrel between sisters, shows one sister leaving, and then reports a later reconciliation.
It introduces a boarding house, lists its residents, and then focuses on one boarder's family history.
items.explanation: 글은 2년간 말하지 않던 자매가 부엌에서 어색하게 다시 만나 서로 불평만 하는 장면으로 시작한다. 이어 Wenhua가 아버지가 서리 든 해에 쓴 오렌지로 마멀레이드를 만든 기억을 꺼내고, 두 사람은 함께 마멀레이드를 만든다. 따라서 긴장된 재회, 공유된 기억, 협력이라는 순서인 A가 정답이다. B는 흉작의 원인 설명이나 과수원 매각이 없고, C는 한 자매가 떠나는 장면이 없으며, D는 하숙인 목록이 나오지 않는다.

items.passage: "Tell the landlord the money is coming from the city," Haoran said, as if it were already true. Baoyu stood at the window of the rented farmhouse outside Chengdu and watched the rain flatten the young rice. His uncle's plan was simple: a lie about a loan that did not exist would buy them one more season, and one good season would pay back everything they owed. Baoyu had agreed at supper. Now, alone, he went over the account book page by page. The figures were his uncle's, written in neat columns, and beside the last entry was a small note in a different ink: Ask Baoyu if this is right. His uncle had not trusted the plan either. When the landlord's bicycle came up the lane, Baoyu set the book on the table and went out to meet him without rehearsing anything.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It describes a farm's history, then traces a landlord's growing suspicion, and then reports a settlement.
It introduces a deceptive plan, follows a nephew's private reconsideration, and then shows him acting.
It presents an argument between relatives, then shifts to a flashback, and then returns to the argument.
It catalogs a family's debts, compares two ways of paying them, and then concludes that both will fail.
items.explanation: 글은 삼촌 Haoran이 존재하지 않는 대출에 관한 거짓말 계획을 말하는 대화로 시작한다. 이어 Baoyu가 혼자 장부를 넘기다 삼촌이 남긴 메모를 발견하며 계획을 다시 생각하고, 마지막에 연습 없이 집주인을 맞으러 나간다. 따라서 계획 소개, 조카의 내적 재고, 행동이라는 순서인 B가 정답이다. A는 집주인의 의심이 전개되지 않고, C는 회상이 없으며, D는 두 상환 방법을 비교하지 않는다.

items.passage: Four duties came with my summer job at the rural post office outside Naples: sort the mail, sell the stamps, lock the safe, and give directions to anyone who wandered down from the hills. I was proud of the fourth. So when a hiker named Matteo stumbled in at dusk, sunburned and lost, I drew him a confident map to the trailhead. An hour later Chiara, the park ranger, brought him back. My map had sent him up the wrong ridge. I expected her to tell him whose fault it was. Instead, she told him the trail signs had been moved by the wind, which was not quite true, and she asked me for a glass of water for him. After he left, she sat with me and redrew the map, slowly, landmark by landmark. I have kept that second map, folded in a drawer, for twenty years.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It lists the narrator's duties, then criticizes the ranger's dishonesty, and then defends the narrator's map.
It describes a long hike in detail, then explains why trail signs often fail, and then recommends better maps.
It sets out the narrator's duties, recounts a mistake a ranger quietly covered, and notes its lasting effect.
It introduces a lost hiker, then shifts to the ranger's own past, and then returns to the narrator's job.
items.explanation: 글은 우체국 일의 네 가지 의무를 나열하며 시작하고, 화자가 자랑하던 길 안내에서 실수를 한 일화를 전한다. 레인저 Chiara는 화자의 실수를 드러내지 않고 바람 탓으로 돌린 뒤 지도를 함께 다시 그려 주며, 화자는 그 지도를 20년간 간직했다고 말한다. 따라서 의무 소개, 숨겨 준 실수, 지속적인 영향의 순서인 C가 정답이다. A는 화자가 레인저를 비판하지 않으며, B는 등산 과정이나 권고가 없고, D는 레인저의 과거가 나오지 않는다.

items.passage: Once, when I was eleven, I asked my father why he had left Japan, and Shigeru only handed me a knife and an onion. That was the beginning of our agreement. In the galley of the fishing boat he cooked for, docked each winter in Hokkaido's colder harbors, we talked in English about everything else: the crew's appetites, the price of squid, my school in Seattle. I translated menus and invoices for him. He taught me to fillet a fish in four strokes. Neither of us mentioned the subject. Then, the winter I turned seventeen, a deckhand asked him the same question I had asked. My father answered in Japanese, at length, while I stood at the cutting board pretending not to understand. I understood every word. That night, Sachiko, he said, you can ask me again. I did not, and I have never been sure whether that silence was kindness or cowardice.
items.question: Which choice best describes the overall structure of the text?
options: It explains why the father emigrated, then describes his galley work, and then praises his cooking.
It compares two languages, then lists the narrator's chores, and then describes a storm.
It narrates a bitter argument between the father and daughter and then reports how they reconciled.
It establishes a long silence, presents an event that disrupts it, and reflects on the outcome.
items.explanation: 글은 화자가 열한 살 때 아버지가 이민 이유에 대한 질문에 답하지 않으면서 생긴 침묵의 약속을 소개한다. 이어 열일곱 살 때 갑판원의 질문에 아버지가 일본어로 길게 답하는 사건이 그 침묵을 깨고, 화자는 다시 묻지 않은 자신의 선택을 돌아본다. 따라서 침묵 설정, 그것을 흔드는 사건, 결과에 대한 성찰의 순서인 D가 정답이다. A는 이민 이유가 화자에게 직접 설명되지 않고, B는 폭풍이 없으며, C는 두 사람이 다투는 장면이 없다.

items.passage: Chalk dust and the sour smell of wet wool filled the tailor's back room in Colombo, where Hassan, the ship's captain, had ordered the stowaway brought for questioning. Imani sat on a bolt of cloth, chin raised. They argued for an hour about a button. She had cut one from his spare coat to trade for bread, and he insisted it was brass from Bombay, worth more than her passage. She insisted it was painted tin. __Neither of them mentioned that she had hidden aboard because her father's boat had not come back, or that Hassan had been the last to see it.__ The tailor, pinning a hem in the corner, said nothing either. Finally Hassan held the button to the lamp, scratched it with his thumbnail, and saw the tin beneath. He set it on the table between them and asked, more gently than before, where she would like to go.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It reveals the deeper grief beneath a quarrel that has so far seemed trivial.
It explains how Imani managed to board the captain's ship without being seen.
It suggests that the tailor knows more about the button than either character.
It confirms that Hassan was right all along about the value of the button.
items.explanation: 밑줄 앞에서 두 사람은 한 시간 동안 단추가 놋쇠인지 양철인지라는 사소한 문제로 다툰다. 밑줄 문장은 Imani가 아버지의 배가 돌아오지 않아 숨어 탔고 Hassan이 그 배를 마지막으로 본 사람이라는 사실을 밝혀, 다툼 밑의 진짜 슬픔을 드러낸다. 그 뒤 Hassan이 더 부드럽게 묻는 결말도 이 기능과 이어지므로 A가 정답이다. B는 승선 방법을 설명하지 않고, C는 재단사에 관한 내용이 아니며, D는 단추가 양철로 드러난다는 결말과 반대다.

items.passage: Oaxaca's Saturday market was nearly closed when Valentina opened the shoebox of their mother's letters on the empty chili stand. Eulalio sat beside her, arms crossed. For years he had blamed her for the scholarship he never took: she had been the one to tell their mother she could not run the stall alone. Valentina read aloud, letter by letter, the weekly accounts of sales and weather. Then she reached one dated the spring of his scholarship. __Their mother had written, in a hand much shakier than usual, that she had asked her daughter to say it, because she could not bear to say it herself.__ Eulalio uncrossed his arms. Neither of them spoke while the vendors folded their awnings. When Valentina moved to close the box, he stopped her and asked her to keep reading, even the letters about the weather.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces the mother's reasons for running the stall alone after the scholarship.
It reveals information that shifts the blame Eulalio has long placed on Valentina.
It suggests that Valentina has invented the letter to defend her earlier choice.
It explains why the mother's weekly letters usually described sales and weather.
items.explanation: 앞부분에서 Eulalio는 장학금을 포기한 일을 오랫동안 누나 Valentina 탓으로 여겨 왔다. 밑줄 문장은 어머니가 스스로 말할 수 없어 딸에게 대신 말하게 했다는 사실을 밝혀, 그 원망의 대상이 잘못되었음을 드러낸다. 이후 Eulalio가 팔짱을 풀고 계속 읽어 달라고 하는 반응도 이를 뒷받침하므로 B가 정답이다. A는 어머니가 혼자 노점을 운영했다는 내용과 맞지 않고, C는 편지를 지어냈다는 근거가 없으며, D는 편지의 일상적 내용을 설명하는 문장이 아니다.

items.passage: After my mother remarried, Anh became the keeper of one rule in our house: no talking in the reading room of the old library in Hanoi, where he took me every Sunday. I resented it. For a year we sat across from each other in silence, he with his newspapers and I, Putri, with whatever novel I could pretend to read. I decided the rule was his way of avoiding me. Then, the week before I left for university, I asked whether the rule still applied now that I was grown. He thought about it, then slid a library slip across the table. On it he had written, in pencil, the title of every book I had read there that year, with a small mark beside the ones I had finished twice. __He had been paying attention the entire time.__ We walked home talking, loudly, the whole way.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It confirms the narrator's early belief that the stepfather avoided her.
It explains why the library enforced strict silence in its reading room.
It states the realization that overturns the narrator's view of the rule.
It introduces a new rule that replaces the one the stepfather once kept firmly.
items.explanation: 화자는 침묵 규칙을 의붓아버지 Anh이 자신을 피하는 방식이라고 여겼다. 그러나 그가 화자가 1년 동안 읽은 모든 책과 두 번 읽은 책까지 적어 둔 쪽지를 내밀자, 밑줄 문장은 그가 내내 관심을 기울이고 있었다는 깨달음을 직접 말한다. 이 깨달음이 규칙에 대한 화자의 기존 해석을 뒤집으므로 C가 정답이다. A는 반대 내용이고, B는 도서관의 정책을 설명하지 않으며, D는 새로운 규칙이 소개되지 않는다.

items.passage: I worked nights at a small clinic near the old stone bridge in Haifa, and Yitzhak was the patient who never slept. He talked instead, mostly about the bridge, which he had crossed every morning for fifty years on his way to the docks. One night his son phoned to say the family had decided to move him to a care home in another city. No one had asked him. I knew because I had been asked to keep it quiet until the papers were signed. I, Chana, said nothing, and for three nights I let him talk about the bridge as if he would walk it again. __On the fourth night I wheeled him to the window and told him.__ He was quiet a long time. Then he asked me to describe the bridge to him in the morning light, so he would have a newer picture to take with him.
items.question: Which choice best describes the function of the underlined sentence in the text as a whole?
options: It introduces the bridge as a place the patient has never seen before.
It shows the narrator following the family's request to delay the news.
It marks the moment when the patient finally learns to sleep through the night.
It marks the narrator's decision to end her silence about the family's choice.
items.explanation: 화자 Chana는 가족이 Yitzhak에게 묻지 않고 요양원 이전을 결정했다는 사실을 서류 서명 전까지 숨기라는 부탁을 받고 사흘 동안 침묵한다. 밑줄 문장은 넷째 날 밤 그녀가 그 침묵을 깨고 사실을 알리는 순간을 보여 준다. 이후 Yitzhak이 다리를 묘사해 달라고 부탁하는 결말도 이 결정에서 이어지므로 D가 정답이다. A는 그가 다리를 50년간 건넜다는 내용과 맞지 않고, B는 부탁을 어기는 장면이므로 반대이며, C는 잠에 관한 변화가 나오지 않는다.

items.passage: Efua had expected the projection booth to smell of dust, but it smelled of oil and warm metal, the way her father's hands once had. Ayesha, who had run the projectors at the small Vermont cinema with him for thirty years, threaded the film without looking, talking the whole time. Most people thought the work was finished, she said; the big theaters had gone digital, and no one needed to know how to splice a broken reel. Efua watched her fingers. They were swollen at the knuckles and moved more slowly than her voice, yet they never missed a sprocket. When the film caught, Ayesha did not curse. She simply stopped the machine, cut the damaged frame, and joined the ends with a patience that seemed almost tender. Efua realized she had come for her father's stories and was staying for this woman's hands.
items.question: Which choice best describes the narrator's attitude toward Ayesha?
options: Pity for Ayesha's aging hands mixed with doubt about her skill
Growing admiration for Ayesha's careful, unhurried craftsmanship
Polite indifference toward Ayesha's work and her stories of the past
Mild irritation at Ayesha's constant talk during the screening
items.explanation: 서술자는 Ayesha의 손가락이 관절이 부어 느려졌지만 톱니 구멍을 한 번도 놓치지 않는다고 묘사한다. 필름이 걸렸을 때도 욕하지 않고 손상된 프레임을 잘라 다정하다 싶을 만큼 참을성 있게 잇는 장면을 세밀히 관찰하고, Efua는 이 여인의 손 때문에 머물게 되었다고 깨닫는다. 따라서 신중하고 서두르지 않는 기술에 대한 점점 커지는 감탄인 B가 정답이다. A는 실력에 대한 의심이 없고, C는 세밀한 관찰과 맞지 않으며, D는 그녀의 말에 대한 짜증이 드러나지 않는다.
